facts.statement: Scaphognathus lived in Germany during the Late Jurassic period.
facts.quote: Scaphognathus was a pterosaur that lived around Germany during the Late Jurassic.

facts.statement: The adult Scaphognathus had a wingspan of 0.9 meters (3 feet).
facts.quote: It had a wingspan of 0.9 m (3 ft).

facts.statement: August Goldfuss first described the species in 1831, initially misidentifying it as Pterodactylus crassirostris.
facts.quote: The first known Scaphognathus specimen was described in 1831 by August Goldfuss who mistook the tailless specimen for a new Pterodactylus species: P. crassirostris.

facts.statement: The specific name crassirostris translates to "fat snout" in Latin.
facts.quote: The specific name means "fat snout" in Latin.

facts.statement: The type specimen was an incomplete adult with a 0.9-meter wingspan found in the Solnhofen strata near Eichstätt.
facts.quote: This specimen was an incomplete adult with a 0.9 m (3 ft) wingspan recovered from the Solnhofen strata near Eichstätt.

facts.statement: Johann Wagner established the genus Scaphognathus in 1861, naming it after the blunt shape of the lower jaws.
facts.quote: In 1861 named a distinct genus: Scaphognathus, derived from Greek skaphe, "boat" or "tub", and gnathos, "jaw", in reference to the blunt shape of the lower jaws.

facts.statement: A second, smaller specimen with a twenty-inch wingspan and partially ossified bones was identified as a juvenile.
facts.quote: The second Scaphognathus specimen was more complete than its predecessor, but only half the size (twenty inch wingspan) and with partially ossified bones. These characters indicate that the second specimen was a juvenile.

facts.statement: Three specimens of Scaphognathus are known, all from the Kimmeridgian-age Solnhofen Limestone.
facts.quote: The Scaphognathus is known from three specimens, all of which originated in the Kimmeridgian-age Solnhofen Limestone.

facts.statement: The teeth of Scaphognathus were oriented vertically rather than horizontally.
facts.quote: Its teeth oriented vertically rather than horizontally.

facts.statement: Comparisons of scleral rings suggest Scaphognathus may have been diurnal.
facts.quote: Comparisons between the scleral rings of Scaphognathus and modern birds and reptiles suggest that it may have been diurnal.

facts.statement: Its potential diurnal nature suggests niche partitioning with contemporary nocturnal pterosaurs like Ctenochasma and Rhamphorhynchus.
facts.quote: This may also indicate niche partitioning with contemporary pterosaurs inferred to be nocturnal, such as Ctenochasma and Rhamphorhynchus.

facts.statement: A 2013 phylogenetic analysis by Andres & Myers placed Scaphognathus within the rhamphorhynchid family tree.
facts.quote: The cladogram (family tree) of rhamphorhynchids below is the result of a large phylogenetic analysis published by Andres & Myers in 2013.

facts.statement: Scaphognathus belongs to the family Rhamphorhynchidae.
The genus Scaphognathus is classified within the subfamily Scaphognathinae.
Scaphognathus lived between 168.2 and 143.1 million years ago, from the Bathonian to the Tithonian stages.
facts.quote: Time range: Bathonian to Tithonian (168.2 to 143.1 million years ago)

facts.statement: The parent group for the genus Scaphognathus is the subfamily Scaphognathinae.

rejected.statement: A second specimen found in Mühlheim in the early 20th century revealed a long tail, confirming the animal's rhamphorhynchoid nature.
rejected.quote: In the early twentieth century, the "rhamphorhynchoid" nature of S. crassirostris was recognized after the discovery of the second specimen in Mühlheim, whose long tail was preserved.

rejected.statement: Scaphognathus possessed a proportionately shorter skull, approximately 4.5 inches long, with a blunter tip and a larger antorbital fenestra.
rejected.quote: For one, Scaphognathus had a proportionately shorter skull (4.5 in) with a blunter tip and a larger antorbital fenestra.
